item.title: Why Our Poll Shows Democrats Leading in the House
item.description: Our polling reporter Ruth Igielnik describes what likely voters told us in the latest Times/Siena poll leading up to this year’s midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Ruth Igielnik, Laura Bult, Thomas Vollkommer, Laura Salaberry, June Kim, Nikolay Nikolov, Rafaela Balster and Whitney Shefte

item.title: With Trump’s Plans Blocked, States Work to Restore Trust in Mail Voting
item.description: President Trump’s efforts to restrict mail voting ahead of the midterms were thwarted by the Supreme Court, but they have sowed confusion and doubt among some voters.
item.dc:creator: Nick Corasaniti, Anna Griffin and Richard Fausset
item.media:credit: Matt Ramey/Associated Press
item.media:description: Election workers preparing absentee ballots this month in Raleigh, N.C.

item.title: Universities Sound Warnings About A.I. Even as They Embrace It
item.description: As A.I. upends education, university leaders have been all over the map about how to respond. It can be very confusing for students.
item.dc:creator: Mark Arsenault, Dana Goldstein, Alan Blinder and Sarah Mervosh
item.media:credit: Philip Cheung for The New York Times
item.media:description: Some university leaders have said schools must embrace A.I. to stay relevant.

item.title: Democrats Gain Midterms Edge as Trump Drags Down Republicans, Per Times/Siena Poll
item.description: Even some Republicans are losing faith in Trump’s economy, a New York Times/Siena poll found, and Democrats were favored on the top issues as the sprint to the midterms gets underway.
item.dc:creator: Shane Goldmacher, Ruth Igielnik and Sophia June
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:credit: Edison Wu/The New York Times

item.title: Alex Bores Wants Democrats to Make AI Safety a 2028 Election Issue
item.description: Alex Bores, who lost a congressional primary contest that revolved around A.I. regulation, is trying to position himself at the center of the conversation for the next presidential election.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Oreskes and Theodore Schleifer
item.media:credit: Heather Khalifa for The New York Times
item.media:description: Alex Bores campaigning in Central Park in June. He lost a Democratic primary contest for the House that centered on A.I. regulation.

item.title: Could a Progressive Democrat Really Become Governor of Texas?
item.description: Gina Hinojosa, a state lawmaker from Austin, challenged Gov. Greg Abbott when no other Democrat would. “I needed to try,” she said.
item.dc:creator: Edgar Sandoval and Christopher Lee
item.media:description: Gina Hinojosa has made support for public schools and concerns about affordability centerpieces of her campaign.

item.title: U.S. Has Deployed Weapons in Space, Air Force Secretary Says
item.description: Troy E. Meink’s comments were the first public acknowledgment of American weapons in orbit. The Pentagon has been preparing for potential conflict in space with Russia or China.
item.dc:creator: Francesca Regalado
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Pool photo by Matt Rourke
item.media:description: Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink speaks during the United States Air Force Academy graduation ceremony in Colorado Springs in May.

item.title: Supreme Court Justices Thomas and Alito Would Have Allowed Trump’s Mail-In Ballot Rules
item.description: Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr., joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, called the challenge to the restrictions a “Hail Mary pass” that was unlikely to prevail because of the Postal Service’s broad authority to regulate the mail.
item.dc:creator: Ann E. Marimow

item.title: Trump’s Effort to Assert Control Over Elections Continues Despite Supreme Court Loss
item.description: President Trump has launched a broad, governmentwide effort to take more control of state-run elections and sow doubt about the outcome.
item.dc:creator: Zolan Kanno-Youngs
item.media:credit: Rebecca Noble for The New York Times
item.media:description: Mail ballots await their mailing date in Phoenix in 2022.

item.title: Elections Officials Breathe Sigh of Relief Following Court Ruling on Mail Ballots
item.description: Officials cheered the order blocking President Trump’s last-minute effort to change the rules on mail ballots, noting that some states had already mailed ballots.
item.dc:creator: Chris Cameron
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: Jena Griswold, the Democratic secretary of state in Colorado, said in a statement that “Trump’s attempt to sabotage the 2026 elections has failed.”

item.title: Judge Blocks Trump Rule Aimed at International Students and Journalists
item.description: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV wrote that the administration’s reasons for a rule limiting the length of stay for academics and journalists were “exceptionally weak.”
item.dc:creator: Chris Cameron
item.media:credit: Lucy Lu for The New York Times
item.media:description: A rally in support of international students at Harvard University last year. The Trump administration rule would have shortened the length of visas for international students, academics and foreign journalists.

item.title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump Administration Plan to Screen Mail-In Ballots
item.description: The Trump administration had asked the justices to allow a new Postal Service plan to screen ballots just weeks before the midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Abbie VanSickle
item.media:credit: Mike Kai Chen for The New York Times
item.media:description: A resident drops off her mail ballot in Livermore, Calif., last month.

item.title: Gavin Newsom Says He Won’t Run in 2028 if Kamala Harris Does
item.description: The comments made to CNN, if taken at face value, seemed to fly in the face of the California governor’s presidential ambitions.
item.dc:creator: Reid J. Epstein
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran and Nick Hagen for The New York Times
item.media:description: Gov. Gavin Newsom of California and former Vice President Kamala Harris are widely seen as potential 2028 presidential candidates.

item.title: Mitch McConnell Returns to Senate After Three Month Absence
item.description: Senator Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old Kentucky Republican and former leader, had been absent for more than 13 weeks after a health incident, fueling questions about his ability to continue serving.
item.dc:creator: Catie Edmondson, Carl Hulse and Michael Gold
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross for The New York Times
item.media:description: Senator Mitch McConnell arriving for a vote at the Capitol on Monday afternoon. He had not been seen there since he last cast a floor vote on June 11.

item.title: As A.I. Fears Rise, Experts Suggest Focusing on the Humans in Charge
item.description: Warnings from industry leaders about doomsday scenarios ignore the power that people have to control how artificial intelligence is used, policy experts say. They are urging lawmakers to act now.
item.dc:creator: Maia Spoto and Jill Cowan
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dario Amodei of Anthropic called for slowing the A.I. development in a 3,800-word essay over the weekend.

item.title: Maduro Ally Is Expected to Plead Guilty in Federal Money Laundering Case
item.description: Alex Saab, a former high-ranking government official in Venezuela, could potentially cooperate against Mr. Maduro, who is awaiting trial in New York.
item.dc:creator: David Ovalle
item.media:credit: Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Reuters
item.media:description: Alex Saab was fired from his post as Venezuela’s industry minister soon after Nicolás Maduro was taken by American special forces in January.

item.title: Political Figures From Bernie Sanders to Steve Bannon Sound Alarms on A.I.
item.description: The two men will appear separately at an event calling for a “pro-human” approach to A.I. as warnings mount from the industry and the technology’s danger becomes a midterm issue.
item.dc:creator: Bayliss Wagner and Neil Vigdor
item.media:credit: Angelina Katsanis and Desiree Rios for The New York Times
item.media:description: Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon.

item.title: Russian Businessman With Putin Ties Paid for Donald Trump Jr.’s Wedding Party
item.description: The payments, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars, represented an extraordinary flouting of ethical norms for an American president’s family member.
item.dc:creator: Ben Protess

item.media:description: The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., accepted the gifts from Umar Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

item.title: An Armadillo Arrives in … Ohio?
item.description: Traditionally found in warm climates, like the American Southwest, armadillos have been migrating farther and farther north, researchers say.
item.dc:creator: Victor Mather
item.media:credit: Aaron Ambos
item.media:description: The armadillo that was found in Ohio, near the Indiana border.

item.title: Why Is D.H.S. Getting Involved in Elections?
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security is in the midst of a weeks-long hunt for noncitizens among the nation’s registered voters despite the absence of evidence of widespread fraud. Reporter Hamed Aleaziz breaks down how a D.H.S. agency is using open-source state voter registration websites in their search for voter fraud.
item.dc:creator: Hamed Aleaziz, Joy Sung, Nikolay Nikolov, Stephanie Swart, June Kim, Rafaela Balster, Alexandra Ostasiewicz and Whitney Shefte

item.title: Whistle-Blower: Federal Agents May Have Broken State Laws in Search For Voter Fraud
item.description: Agents expressed concern about being directed by top Homeland Security leaders to use private information to look up voter records in state databases.
item.dc:creator: Nick Corasaniti and Hamed Aleaziz
item.media:credit: Matt Gade/Associated Press
item.media:description: New citizens registered to vote following a naturalization ceremony at Mount Rushmore in South Dakota last year.

item.title: Vance Campaigns in Kansas as Democrats Target a Republican Stronghold
item.description: Vice President JD Vance is beginning a key final stretch of midterm campaigning by dropping in on the Senate race in Kansas, where Republicans were long seen as heavily favored.
item.dc:creator: Jess Bidgood
item.media:credit: Pool photo by Mark Schiefelbein
item.media:description: Vice President JD Vance is one of Republicans’ most valuable surrogates on the campaign trail.

item.title: Immigrants’ Lawyers Say U.S. Is Redacting Documents Proving Legal Status
item.description: Many noncitizens need immigration records the government has to prove their legal stay and resist deportation. The government is redacting and withholding those documents, lawyers say.
item.dc:creator: Minho Kim
item.media:credit: Alan Nakkash for The New York Times
item.media:description: Federal law mandates that agencies provide immigrants facing deportations needed documents “pertaining to the alien’s admission or presence.”

item.title: Trump Rejects Talk of A.I. Regulation and Calls Out Anthropic’s CEO
item.description: The president again rejected calls to try to regulate the industry, even as some of its leaders are speaking more openly about the risks of rapidly developing artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Swan and Michael Gold
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump has spent much of his second term aligning himself with promoters of artificial intelligence who have been pushing the U.S. government to clear away obstacles to growth.

item.title: States and Cities Sue Over Trump’s Policy to Restrict Green Cards
item.description: The policy would give immigration officers wide authority to deny green cards to people using public benefits.
item.dc:creator: Madeleine Ngo
item.media:credit: Angela Weiss/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: “Denying people services does not erase their need; it compounds it,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York said at a news conference on Monday, alongside Attorney General Letitia James.

item.title: Key West Feels the Pain of Trump Decision on Haitians
item.description: The end of legal protections for Haitian immigrants nationally has jolted the labor market in this remote vacation destination in Florida where many live and work.
item.dc:creator: David Ovalle
item.media:credit: Mark Hedden for The New York Times
item.media:description: A Haitian immigrant who works at a supermarket in Key West leaves home less often since losing Temporary Protected Status in July.

item.title: As Supreme Court Weighs Trump Mail Ballot Plan, Another Judge Blocks It
item.description: The ruling by a lower court judge was another blow to President Trump’s effort to make voting by mail harder. The Supreme Court is also considering the Trump plan.
item.dc:creator: Zach Montague
item.media:credit: Alisha Jucevic for The New York Times
item.media:description: The ruling was the second by a federal district judge to find that President Trump’s mail ballot plan is likely illegal.

item.title: ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ Used Small Cages to Confine Migrants, DHS Watchdog Report Says
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security’s internal watchdog provided new details about conditions at the now-shuttered Florida detention center.

item.media:credit: Doug Mills/The New York Times
